Bellingcat February Challenges

Exploring Extremist Symbolism

Bellingcat Challenges February

Introduction

This blog post will show how I solved the February OSINT Challenges from Bellingcat. I did these challenges over two days.

Iconography of Hate

I recently saw that Bellingcat published a website that goes into different symbols to describe hate. I figured this would be a good start to solve this challenge. Thus, I went to the Bellingcat Monitoring Glossary, and looked under the visual symbols tab. I opened all the symbols and looked at which one matched.

Symbols 2, 3, 6 were present in the Monitoring Glossary, thus, 2, 3, 6 is the answer.

Fascist Echoes

This challenge is more complicated than the first one. First, I need to identify the logo, then figure out when the weapon on which the logo is displayed was used, and finally see what law changed when.

I happen, because of my addiction to reading the news, and my studies, to know that this is likely the weapon used in the Christchurch shooting. But first I went to read up on the symbol. According to the Bellingcat Monitoring Glossary, the symbol was used in the Christchurch shooting and was first used by the Iron Guard movement. Looks like I have found the second part of the question already.

I remember when the Christchurch shooting happened, and I recalled that the government in New Zealand changed many gun-related laws. Using this as my starting point, Google AI overview showed that indeed parliament quickly passed laws and changed the legislation.

But I wanted a specific date. The Firearms Safety Authority shows all the relevant information. Here I found the answer to the puzzle: On 12/04/2019 the Arms Amendment Act 2019 became law in New Zealand.

Symbolic Literacy

This challenge took me a couple of hours. Here’s what I did:

First I looked at the image. It shows some kind of old fortification, with a graffiti mark visible. There is some metadata available, namely a date and time. At first glance, the fortification seems to be older (pre cold-war) and in Europe.

But I needed to first focus on the graffiti. It took me a while to figure this out. I tried to Google Lens it, to describe and google it in various forms, to draw it and Google lens my drawing. I went through all the symbols on the Bellingcat Monitoring Glossary. I went through a bunch of right-wing extremist symbols on Wikipedia and a German Government list, but I couldn’t find it still.

Then, I went back to the Bellingcat Monitoring Glossary and I went through all the pages. The last page provided me a crucial hint, when I wasn’t really expecting it anymore. Apparently, the logo that is visible on the wall is associated with the Ustase, a Croatian fascist movement.

Next, I went to ChatGPT. Usually not that useful, but I wanted to narrow down my search area. The text-generator “explained” to me that this logo is almost exclusively used in Croatia, and to a lesser extent in the Croatian parts of Bosnia.

I went to Google Maps and searched for “Bunker”. The results were not useful to me. Then I Googled for lists of bunkers in Croatia. The results were also not right, although some bunkers looked quite similar but were different in layout. I contemplated looking at the shadows and calculating the latitude to narrow down my search, but I felt I could probably find it faster a different way.

I went to Google translate and translated the words for bunker, ustase and graffiti. I created the following search query: “bunker” AND “ustaše” AND “grafiti”. The second hit included images that looked promising to me.

Scrolling down that page I found a picture of the doorway that looked exactly like the photo in the challenge. The graffiti changed, but the shape of the doorway has a very recognizable cutout on the top-left. Note that the new graffiti is still anti-semitic, even though it’s different. I can see the answer on this webpage too.

The location is Vila Rebar, and it was once the home of the Fascist leader of Croatia called Pavelić, also known as the Butcher of the Balkans. The Villa burned down in 1979, and they apparently never rebuilt it.

Far-right Fashion

I could answer this question immediately. After my adventures in the previous challenges I read up on so many symbols I could instantly see that this logo is a stylized version of the Fasces. This can also be seen in the Bellingcat Monitoring Glossary, but then in Graffiti form.

Fixed Narrative

A slightly different challenge, and a very easy one again. I need to find the location of the sticker and decipher what symbol is used in the sticker.

For the location, I Googled Lensed the building visible on the left. This led me to an Instagram page which mentioned “Belgrade” as the location. The building matches perfectly, such as how the antennae on the top of the building are located.

The visible symbol is the “Celtic Cross”, as can be seen in the Bellingcat Monitoring Glossary. Combining this, I found the answer: Belgrade, Celtic Cross.

This month, the challenges were rather easy, but fun to do still. I cannot wait till next month!
